title: Comparisons of the Distributions for One Quantitative Variable
rights: Original instructor-authored exercises only. No College Board question, figure or scoring key reproduced.

items.prompt: Two classes recorded daily screen time in minutes. Class X has 20 students and Class Y has 80. Which graph best compares the shapes of the time distributions without confusing different sample sizes?
items.hint: Ask which display uses a common unit, matching intervals and proportions rather than unequal raw counts.
items.solution: C. Relative-frequency histograms use the same measurement, common bin boundaries and relative heights, so group size does not determine the bar heights.
items.provenance: Original Maple Hill School hypothetical question, 2026-10-15

options.label: A
options.text: Two histograms of raw frequency, one with 5-minute bins and one with 20-minute bins.

options.label: B
options.text: Two bar charts of class names showing the number of students.

options.label: C
options.text: Two relative-frequency histograms with equal 5-minute bins on a common time axis.

options.label: D
options.text: Two pie charts showing just each class's total minutes.

items.prompt: Route A has 12 journey times with median 16.5 minutes, IQR 3 minutes and a fairly balanced dotplot. Route B has 12 times with median 13.5 minutes, IQR 5 minutes and a pronounced high right tail, including 38 minutes. Write a three-sentence comparison containing center, variability and one feature of shape or unusual observations.
items.hint: Write a sentence that directly compares the two groups rather than independently describing each. Quantify two differences.
items.solution: Route B's sample median journey time is 3 minutes shorter (13.5 versus 16.5), but its middle-half journey times vary more (IQR 5 versus 3 minutes). Route B has a long right tail and unusually high 38-minute trip, whereas A is more balanced. These observations describe the sampled trips only; they do not show that riding B causes a shorter trip.
items.provenance: Original Maple Hill School hypothetical question, 2026-10-15
items.rubric: Award credit for named groups and minutes, correct median comparison/difference, correct IQR comparison, justified tail or outlier feature, and no unsupported causal claim.

items.prompt: In the route example, median A = 16.5 minutes and median B = 13.5 minutes. By how many minutes is A's median LONGER than B's? Enter a positive number.
items.hint: Subtract the median for Route B from the median for Route A; units are minutes.
items.solution: $16.5-13.5=3$ minutes. This is the difference between sample medians, not a statement about every individual's journey.
items.provenance: Original Maple Hill School hypothetical question, 2026-10-15

items.prompt: Two numerical samples have identical five-number summaries. Which statement is still possible?
items.hint: A boxplot compresses many observations into just a few numbers. Imagine different interior arrangements.
items.solution: B. The samples may have very different modes or gaps even with matching five-number summaries; a dotplot or histogram is needed to see those.
items.provenance: Original Maple Hill School hypothetical question, 2026-10-15

options.label: B
options.text: One may be bimodal while the other is unimodal.

options.label: C
options.text: Both must come from normal populations.

options.label: D
options.text: They must have identical numerical observations in the same order.

items.prompt: On an assessment, the population mean is 70 points and population SD is 8 points. A student's score is 86 points. Compute the population-referenced z-score.
items.hint: Subtract the population mean from the observed score, then divide by population SD.
items.solution: $z=\frac{86-70}{8}=2$. The score is two population SDs above the mean; z has no units.
items.provenance: Original Maple Hill School hypothetical question, 2026-10-15

items.prompt: At a workplace, the population mean travel time is 85 minutes with population SD 6 minutes. An employee takes 73 minutes. Compute the employee's z-score.
items.hint: A value below the mean should produce a negative standardized distance.
items.solution: $z=\frac{73-85}{6}=-2$. This journey is two population SDs below the population mean. The sign is negative; z is unit-free.
items.provenance: Original Maple Hill School hypothetical question, 2026-10-15

items.prompt: A student scores 86 on Assessment A (population mean 70, SD 8) and 90 on Assessment B (population mean 80, SD 10). Which statement compares the relative positions correctly?
items.hint: Evaluate (x − population mean)/population SD for each test, then compare, not the raw scores.
items.solution: A. The z-scores are $z_A=2$ and $z_B=1$. A's score is farther above its own population mean in standard-deviation units, despite the lower raw score.
items.provenance: Original Maple Hill School hypothetical question, 2026-10-15

options.label: A
options.text: The score on A is farther above its reference mean in SD units.

options.label: B
options.text: The score on B has a higher z-score because 90 > 86.

options.label: C
options.text: Both z-scores equal 1 because the student is above average on both.

options.label: D
options.text: One cannot calculate either z-score from these population summaries.

items.prompt: Two reference populations both have mean 50 and standard deviation 10, but one is strongly right-skewed while the other is approximately symmetric. A score of 60 has $z=1$ in both. Does this prove that 60 is at the same percentile in both populations? Explain.
items.hint: Standardizing measures distance from the mean. What else determines the fraction of values below a score?
items.solution: No. Both scores are 10 units above their respective mean, which is one standard deviation in each population. But a percentile is determined by the shape of each entire distribution—the fraction of observations at or below 60. Different shapes can give different cumulative proportions at the same z-score; z-scoring does not transform either distribution to normal.
items.provenance: Original Maple Hill School hypothetical question, 2026-10-15
items.rubric: Correctly state no, recognize both standardized distances equal +1, explain that percentile depends on cumulative distribution shape and cannot be inferred from mean and SD alone.

items.prompt: A population has mean 60 points and population SD 4 points. What RAW score has $z=-1.5$? Enter the score in points.
items.hint: Rearrange $x=\mu+z\sigma$; a negative z means the raw score is below the mean.
items.provenance: Original Maple Hill School hypothetical question, 2026-10-15

items.prompt: Someone reads the two route samples and writes: ‘Because Route B's median is three minutes shorter, switching everyone from A to B will cause each person's travel time to drop by three minutes.’ Explain TWO logically separate problems with this claim, and state a supported descriptive conclusion.
items.hint: Does a difference of medians predict each individual's value? Does an observational comparison establish a causal effect?
items.solution: First, a difference between sample medians is a comparison of group summaries, not a three-minute saving for every rider—journey times overlap and vary substantially. Second, without an appropriate randomized or otherwise justified causal design, observed groups cannot show that changing routes causes a reduction. Supported descriptive claim: in the two samples, B's median is 13.5 minutes compared with A's 16.5 minutes (three minutes lower), while B has greater IQR (5 versus 3 minutes) and an unusually long high trip.
items.provenance: Original Maple Hill School hypothetical question, 2026-10-15
items.rubric: Credit both group-versus-individual limitation and causal-inference limitation distinctly; include a correct in-context descriptive comparison with numbers and units.
